quote: Individual organisms are best thought of as adaptation-executers rather than as fitness-maximizers.
content: This is one of the soundest ideas in the sequence. The distinction between the ultimate (selective-historical) cause of a trait and its proximate moment-to-moment operation is Mayr's classic separation of cause in biology (1961) and part of Tinbergen's four questions (1963); confusing the two is a standard error the framework was designed to prevent. No serious caveat applies to the core thesis itself—the caveats below concern the specific stories told to illustrate it.

quote: Micronutrients that were reliably abundant in leaves and nuts are absent from bread
content: The general logic—tastes tuned to past scarcity now firing in an environment of abundance—is sound, but the confident picture of a single ancestral diet is shakier than it sounds. There was no one "environment of evolutionary adaptedness": hominin diets varied enormously by region, season, and epoch, so claims about what was "reliably abundant" are reconstructions, not measurements. The thrifty-gene account of modern obesity that this framing invites is itself disputed—Speakman's "drifty gene" critique (2008) argues the data fit relaxed selection on body weight better than positive selection for fat storage. The mismatch idea is plausible; the specific dietary backstory carries more certainty than the evidence warrants.
